utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, ladies and gentlemen, the technical booth, the interpreters; good morning, the Prosecution; good morning to the Defence. I see that we do not have General Krstic with us today. Madam Registrar, could you inform us what's happening first?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I received a call early this morning that General Krstic would not be present. Apparently, he has a doctor's appointment this morning, and we weren't informed of that. So I requested a written waiver to be sent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Petrusic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours, Mr. President. An appointment that should have taken place yesterday, for reasons unknown to us, was not kept so that this appointment with the doctor has been postponed for today, according to the information we received from the head of the Detention Unit, and that is the reason for the absence of General Krstic at today's hearing. And he has given his approval that the hearing may be held in his absence; that is, he waives his right to be present.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Petrusic. I should like to ask the registrar to check what is happening because, when General Krstic has medical consultations, they should be organised well so that he is able to attend his own trial. So please take care of that. So good morning, General Radinovic. We hope to be able to release you today, and in order to do that, we will work hard. So, Mr. Cayley, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours, counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Good morning, General. Do you hear me, General?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: General, I'd like you to turn, please, to page 52 of your report. That's Defence Exhibit 160.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If page 52 could be placed on the ELMO. I'm interested in paragraph 3.4. THE USHER: Page 32?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Page 52, Mr. Usher, and it's page 52 in the original version.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: 3.4, General. And I'm interested in the penultimate sentence of that paragraph, and here you are referring to the ideal time for the assumption of responsibility of command of the Drina Corps, and you refer to conditions of transfer, and you state, and I quote: "These conditions primarily mean pause or respite in the fighting, and in this case it meant waiting for the end of Operation Zepa, which was in full flow between July 15 and 20." General, do you stand by that portion of your report?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I stand by my report to the effect that the operation started on the 14th and that it was ongoing. This was the period when the Zepa operation was ongoing.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And there was, in your opinion, a lull on the 20th, was there, on the 20th of July?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I didn't investigate the Zepa operation by hour and by day, but in view of the decree that General Krstic received to take over duty of Drina Corps Commander, the most appropriate time was looked for, and I assume that time was the 20th since that was when it actually took place, because, for that type of activity, the most suitable time is sought. So if there is a lull on the battlefront, the conditions warrant the possibility of such a meeting. As you know, documents went to the commands of units to see what time would suit them best for the takeover of duty. Some said the 23rd would be appropriate; some, some other date; but probably the commander of the Main Staff and the commander of the Drina Corps judged that this was the most suitable date, that is, the 20th, when this ceremony took place, an act marking the handing over and taking over of duty and the presence of certain officers of a certain rank as prescribed in the rules of service of the army of Republika Srpska and in the former JNA whose principle provisions were taken over by those rules.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: General, General, as is tradition, you are wandering away from the question that I actually asked you. Are you aware, General, that General Krstic himself stated - and this is in page 6265 of the transcript - that the operation in Zepa was constant up until the 2nd of August? Are you aware? Have you read that evidence?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have read it, but the constancy of an operation does not mean that its intensity is the same every day and every hour. There was this obligation to transfer duty on the basis of the decree of the president of the Republic, and a date was looked for when this could take place. Since it did take place on the 20th, I have no reason not to believe that the conditions were the most appropriate at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: General, if General Krstic stated that fighting was constant between the 15th of July and the 2nd of August, there was no respite in the fighting, was there, in order for the transfer to take place on the 20th in accordance with your theory in paragraph 3.4 of your report, was there, General?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have a key event, that is, the transfer of duty on the 20th. That is a fact that has been proven without any doubt, that that is when this event took place. Since the event did take place and the Zepa operation continued, I assume that that was the most suitable time.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: General, please answer my question, and I'll repeat it for you, because we have to get finished today. General, if the fighting was constant between the 15th of July and the 2nd of August, there was no respite in the fighting, was there, in Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. order for the transfer to take place on the 20th of July in accordance with the theory that you have set out in paragraph 3.4 of your report?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, the fighting does not continue with the same intensity throughout that period. There is lower intensity, regrouping of forces, the introduction of new units, manoeuvring in defence, manoeuvring on the offensive. So whether the greatest pause was on the 20th, I don't know; I wasn't there. But in view of the fact that this transfer took place on the 20th, I assume that there was a lull in the sense of lower intensity and a lesser need for General Krstic to be in Zepa on that date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, but according to your theory, that means that it was possible to envisage lower intensity of combat, but one cannot programme that. To have that ceremony, several people have to be invited to attend on a particular date and at a particular time; and I believe, but you are the expert, that it is not possible to programme fighting in advance and to know in advance that it would be of lower intensity on a particular date. You see, that is the difficulty I'm having.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since the party on the offensive has the initiative, it is possible to plan the intensity or lower intensity for particular days, to delay the introduction of other units, reserve units to lower the intensity of operations. Of course, that does not depend exclusively on the attacker; it also depends on the defender.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, that's an answer. I'm sorry, I have to give the Prosecutor his time, so thank you very much. Mr. Cayley, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: General, if you would please look at paragraph 3.5 of your report.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And if you could move the report up, please, Mr. Usher.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: General, if you would be so good as to read the final sentence of paragraph 3.5, please.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "It has been undeniably established that General Krstic assumed the duty of Drina Corps Commander on July 20, 1995, and this was properly recorded."

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: General, have you seen that record of the takeover of command on the 20th of July?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I was working on my report, I was told that a record was made and that it does exist. I believed it would be no problem to find it, and in the final analysis, I thought that General Krstic would have that record because whoever hands over duty and takes over duty takes a copy of those minutes. I really don't understand how those minutes could have disappeared because it is an official document inaugurating a new situation in the command. However, there are living witnesses who have testified and confirmed that indeed that ceremony took place on the 20th. So I personally have not had that record in my hands, but I trusted General Krstic's statement and the statements of others who testified about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: General, who told you that that record, who told you that that record contained the date the 20th of July? Can you give me the name of that person?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could give you several names if that is absolutely necessary to mention those names here in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Yes. Let's -- we'll have those names in open session. You can give me those names of individuals who saw in that document the date of 20th of July of 1995.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not saying that they saw that document. I'm saying that they attended the ceremony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Visnjic, what is the objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I have no objection. I'm withdrawing my objection.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't say that they saw the record but they were present at that ceremonial transfer of duty.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Do you know of anybody that actually saw that record with the date the 20th of July in it, anybody at all, General?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A record is not shown to people attending a meeting. A record is kept in the archives and copies are giving to the person handing over and the person taking over duty to sign. It is not a document distributed to all.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, General, you've spoken to Defence counsel and you're aware from Mr. Petrusic that he has, in fact, confirmed that that record is missing, the record of hand-over. Did you receive that information from Mr. Petrusic and Mr. Visnjic that the record is missing?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I didn't investigate that. I asked for the record to be given to me from the Defence documents and they didn't, and they told me that it was missing. I asked where the record was, and they told me that in some strange circumstances it had disappeared. I don't mean here in the Tribunal, but it simply is missing. That's what I was told.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Cayley, excuse me. In principle, General, how many copies should exist of such a document? You said that one should go to General Krstic, the other to General Zivanovic, and a third to the archives. Should there be three copies?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There should have been three, yes. There must have been at least three and maybe even more. Then there should be a copy in the archives of the Main Staff as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And it so happens that all these three or more copies have disappeared.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I must admit that I did not find the documents of the Main Staff. I don't know where they are, and I was unable to gain access to them. It is possible that in the Main Staff archives such a document exists, but I have no access to those archives except what the Defence has.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but General Krstic, according to you, should have a copy.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. A copy is given to him. This record on the hand-over is a document on the basis of which he gains certain benefits, not only in terms of command but also in material, financial terms. He acquires certain personal rights referring to that document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand. Thank you very much. Please continue, Mr. Cayley.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, General, you'd agree with me that this is an absolutely fundamental document. Did you make inquiry with General Zivanovic to see whether he had his copy of this document?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't make any inquiries. When I contacted General Zivanovic, at the time there was no question in my mind. I thought that it would be easy to find the document. I did discuss with him the Srebrenica operation, and this was in February or March this year.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: So you spoke with General Zivanovic in February or March of this year, and you never asked to see his copy of the hand-over/takeover document for the Drina Corps Command?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I didn't address that problem with that. I discussed with him the strategic and operational aspect of the operation. He was Corps Commander, and that is the type of contact I had with him. I didn't check about that document. I never thought it would be a problem. When you take the registration book of documents and look up the date July 1995, it should be very easy to trace a document. Unfortunately, I was unable to do that because I did not find the archives of the Main Staff at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, and having learnt that the record was not in the archives, did you try to contact General Zivanovic again to see whether he had a copy?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I lost contact with General Zivanovic. Where I used to contact him, he is no longer there. I really don't know where he is. He may not be in Yugoslavia any more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: General, since this issue was really an important one, did you pursue your inquiry to know what became of this document and what lay behind this disappearance, being aware of all the circumstances? Was there anything behind it? It looks like an intrigue.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, in my inquiries and investigations, I looked for the date when General Krstic took over the duty of Corps Commander and, quite frankly speaking, my interest focussed on when that was rather than on whether the paper exists, so in my preparations for my testimony and the finalisation of my report, I had hoped that I would find it. Perhaps that is my mistake. I actually assumed that somebody else should see to it, to find that document. So believe me, I assumed that in the Prosecution archives, among the Prosecution documents, this document existed, and that they would find it, just as they successively produced numerous documents in the course of these proceedings. I'm really sorry that I didn't look into this matter more thoroughly to be able to answer this question properly, but I thought it was more important to establish the actual date - and we have the live witnesses who actually attended that ceremony - than to focus on the document. I wish I had found it, but unfortunately I have not, and I'm unable to answer your question. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: General, in your discussion --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: In your discussion with General Zivanovic, did you ever ask him directly when he relinquished his command, on what date he stopped being commander? Leaving the document and the handover ceremony aside.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: You didn't -- in your conversation with him, you didn't ask him, even though it was apparent in February or March from the early pre-trial documents of the Prosecution that this was a critical point for them, you didn't ask him when he stopped being commander?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had no doubt in my mind that he was Drina Corps Commander during the Srebrenica operation, and I focussed my attention on that operation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Were you aware that he had given an interview to a magazine that some -- I'm sorry, I don't have it in front of me, at some point in which he himself had placed his leaving the corps at a much earlier date than the 20th?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't know that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: All right. So just to tie this down, you and he never discussed specifically when he said he stopped being commander. That's what you just said; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did not discuss it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, excuse me, another question for you. If I understood you correctly, you said that your concern was the date, to find out that date. Is that correct? Have I understood you properly?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My concern, yes, was to establish the date when General Krstic became Corps Commander because the assessment of his responsibility depends on that fact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So it is as of that date it is possible to establish his responsibility. But my question is, as an expert witness, an experienced military man, the director of investigations, you have engaged in a great deal of research; doesn't it seem to you to be normal when looking for a date to find the document, above all when you knew that there was a trial? I'm sorry, when you know that there's a record, going for the archives, a copy for the person handing over and the person taking over duty. So if your concern was the date, wasn't it normal to find the document? Wouldn't that be the first thing to do? What do you think?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course it is important. It's very important, but from previous contacts I had had with people who attended that ceremony, members of the Main Staff, I had Krstic's testimony --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry for interrupting you, General, but wouldn't it have been more useful for you as an expert - you knew you would be coming here to speak to the Judges - to say to the Judges, "Your Honours, I have the document," instead of saying, "I spoke to this or that or four or five or ten people who were present," and to tell us that they told you that that was the date. Wouldn't it have been preferable to bring the document to the Judges and say, "Here, Your Honours, here are the minutes"? You're telling us that you were primarily concerned with the date, but you didn't make an effort to find the document. Am I understanding you right?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unfortunately, no. This did concern me a great deal as my approach was a step-by-step approach. I first wanted to establish the crucial facts for me, or the relevant facts. A relevant fact for me was that, according to his testimony and what people I spoke to told me before coming here, I established the fact that General Krstic became Corps Commander on the 20th, and then I started working on my research.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry for interrupting you once again. Did you ask General Krstic whether he had his document?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have had no personal contact with General Krstic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But did you take steps to find out whether he had such a document?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Through the Defence, I did ask for this document to be given to me, and it was not given to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Why?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably because they don't have it, either; otherwise, there would be no reason why they wouldn't give it to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So General Krstic's copy has disappeared. It so happens that the document that General Zivanovic could have had, you have lost contact with him. It is not to be found in the archives, and then all in all, all the copies have disappeared. Is that what you are trying to tell us?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm just trying to tell you that I do not have that document. I'm sorry, I regret not having it, but I don't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you very much, General. Mr. Cayley.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: So, General, in conclusion, the archive copy is missing, General Krstic's copy is missing, and you don't know whether General Zivanovic has his copy or not. And I would put it to you, General, that the reason for that is because that document says the 13th of July of 1995, doesn't it, rather than the 20th of July of 1995?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not agree with you because it's not just the probative value of a document. It is not just the document that has probative value, but also what all the people who are familiar with the situation say. I didn't say that it has disappeared from the archives; I said that I didn't gain access to the archives of the Main Staff. I'm sure that it exists there, but to me, it is inaccessible. I have no access to those archives.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: We'll move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If we could have, please, Prosecutor's Exhibit 609, please, Mr. Usher. You were adjusting the heating. It is a little chilly, isn't it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, General, this is a document with which you are familiar and on which you have commented, and if I could just encapsulate your comments on this document. You interpreted -- your opinion was, one, from this document that Lieutenant Colonel Pandurevic knew that there were prisoners in his area of responsibility. Do you recall concluding that from this document? Could you say yes because --

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And, secondly, you interpret this document as stating, or your opinion was that he was using brigade resources to secure those prisoners and clear the terrain. You came to that conclusion. Do you recall?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't understand the second half of your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: In your professional opinion to the Judges, you came to the conclusion from this document that the Brigade Commander, Lieutenant Colonel Pandurevic, was using parts of the Zvornik Brigade to secure prisoners and clear the terrain.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not to clear the terrain. I didn't say that. That does not follow from this document. But that brigade resources were used to secure the prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Your third conclusion from this document was that Colonel Pandurevic did not know that all of the prisoners, by the 15th of July of 1995, had been liquidated. He did not know that fact. That was your interpretation of this document.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, General, the Judges in this case have heard that there were a large number of Muslim men who were executed at a place called Orahovac on the 14th of July of 1995. Are you aware of that fact?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, General, are you also aware that the Prosecutor in this case has presented to the Court records showing that ten members of the Zvornik military police were present in Orahovac on the 14th of July of 1995?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And are you aware that it is the Prosecutor's contention, position, that those members of the military police were guarding the prisoners in Orahovac? Are you aware of that fact?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am aware of that fact, that that is the submission of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Are you also aware, General, that that record showing the presence of those military police in Orahovac was altered, was altered in order to conceal their presence at that location?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am aware that some markings were changed, but whether it was to conceal their presence there it would be difficult for me to say, but I am aware of the contention of the Prosecutor to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: General, secondly, are you aware that a survivor from the Orahovac execution site identified one of his executioners, his would-be executioners, by name? Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have read the testimony. I am aware of it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And you're aware that the individual who that witness identified was identified by the Prosecutor as a member of the 4th Battalion of the Zvornik Brigade? Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Lastly, General, are you aware, thirdly, that the Prosecutor has presented evidence in this case to show that the Zvornik Brigade Engineering Unit was also in Orahovac and that witnesses -- the witness who survived the execution site there stated that there were large vehicles with lights shining on the execution site? Are you aware of that evidence, General?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am aware of that testimony as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: General, if all of those three facts that I've stated to you are true, would you not agree with me that the Brigade Commander, Lieutenant Colonel Pandurevic, on the 15th of July, could not have possibly not known about the fact that Zvornik Brigade military assets were being used for the liquidation of Muslim prisoners? Wouldn't you agree with that, General?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree with you partially, but I disagree in one respect, and that is what I have conveyed to Mr. Visnjic, the Defence attorney. This is a report which Lieutenant Colonel Pandurevic, the Commander of the Zvornik Brigade, made on his return from Zepa. From the context of this report, it can be seen that he does know. He knows that there are prisoners in his zone and that he feels that this is engaging his resources and that he cannot continue. If he had known that they had been liquidated, he would not have put that in this document because it is incriminating. It is in his area of responsibility, and whatever happens in his area of responsibility, he is aware he would be responsible for, and he would not incriminate himself in that way. So on that basis, I came to the conclusion that at that point in time, he did not know that there had been an execution. Rather than wishing on my part to relieve him of any responsibility because that is his -- not only his responsibility, but it would be anybody else's responsibility in the chain of command of the Drina Corps, but I'm claiming that at that point in time he did not know, which doesn't mean that he didn't find out later on. That is my interpretation of this document. So there is no substantive disagreement between you and me on this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: General, this has a sent/received stamp of 1925 hours on the 15th of July. The prisoners have been liquidated by the 14th of July, by the evening, and the burial process was ongoing. Are you stating to the Judges that, by the end of the day on the 15th of July, Colonel Pandurevic had absolutely no idea what his engineers were doing, what his military police were doing, and what one of his battalions within his brigade was doing; that he had no clue what those three units had been doing? Is that your evidence?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That is not what I am saying. I'm claiming, sir, that Lieutenant Colonel Pandurevic, Commander of the Zvornik Brigade, was at Zepa on the 14th and that he was not in the zone of responsibility at that time and that at that time he did not know what was happening in the zone of responsibility. He returned to his zone of responsibility on the 15th, and he was interested first and foremost as there was a crisis in the zone of responsibility of the Zvornik Brigade. That's why he returned. He was primarily interested in --

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: General, in Colonel Pandurevic's absence, who was commanding the brigade? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Chief of Staff was in command of the brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Don't you think, General, that when Colonel Pandurevic returned to Zvornik that somebody briefed him, somebody told him - the Chief of Staff, anybody in the headquarters - as to what was going on in the area of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time that Vinko Pandurevic was at Zepa, his Chief of Staff dealt with all the major -- dealt with the major operative problem in Snagovo where there was a conflict between the forces of the 28th Division and parts of the Zvornik Brigade. And his Chief of Staff, that is to say the deputy commander, was not in the areas in which the executions had allegedly occurred, and it is certain that the Brigade Commander and Chief of Staff, as his deputy, at that time could not have known about it because they were busy with quite different matters and were not aware of that fact. That, of course, cannot free them of responsibility, but I'm trying to explain the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: General, are you aware also on the 14th of July that a mass execution took place at the dam near Petkovci? Are you aware of that fact?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am aware of that fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And are you aware, General, that the Prosecutor has demonstrated that members of the 6th Battalion of the Zvornik Brigade were at Petkovci on the 15th of July?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I read that finding by Mr. Butler, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: General, who is deploying all of these individuals? Give me a name. What was the name of the person? If it wasn't the Chief of Staff and it wasn't the commander of the Zvornik Brigade, who was giving them orders to deploy to these locations, to Orahovac and Petkovci?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, taking care of prisoners is not a problem that the operative part of the command deals with. The care of prisoners of war is something that is seen to by the security system, the security organ and the military police, or rather, the civilian police. And it is quite possible and it is quite probable, indeed, that at the time that this took place, the officers dealing with operative command, that is to say --

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: General --

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- in charge of the combat operations --

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: -- who were the people who were giving the orders? Give me the name or names.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not on the spot for me to be able to know who implemented the orders, executed orders. I'm just saying that why Pandurevic and Obrenovic need not have known that on the 14th and 15th, the executions had taken place. I'm not saying that the executions did not take place. What I'm saying is that the situation in the area of responsibility of the Zvornik Brigade was such that it could have happened, and it was quite probable that it happened. At that moment when they made this report, they did not know about the executions. They were not aware of them; otherwise, they would not have written that down in this report. The information would have gone through different channels and not in an open system of communications in the system of command which is accessible to everyone, because the document itself -- a document itself is the greatest accusation of the command system in whose area of responsibility the executions took place, and they did not know about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: So your evidence is that Colonel Pandurevic was aware of all of these prisoners all over the brigade area of responsibility, but had absolutely no idea whatsoever that most of his brigade was actually involved in murdering these people on the 14th and 15th of July. Is that your evidence?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am quite certain that on the day he wrote the report, at the moment he wrote the report, he did not know about it, but later on quite certainly he did learn of it. He must have learnt of it, but at that point when he wrote this, he did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, General --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Can I just ask one question?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Of course, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: I know this is irritating, to use a word to -- turnabout is fair play. What I don't understand, General, is in this very dispatch that we're discussing here, Pandurevic says, you know, "We can't handle this," and he said, "I will have to let them go." And he also discusses, I think, although it's not high enough on the screen, that there are negotiations going on, presumably with him and the Muslim army, as to creating a corridor through which people will be let go. Now, is it possible to have an army which allows a person in command of a brigade to be negotiating with the opposite army and to believe that he is in control of what's happening to the prisoners when he says, "I will have to let them go," at the same time that a phantom command structure is off liquidating the prisoners? I mean, you're a military expert and you talk about military principles. How can you run an army like that, that a General or a Colonel thinks he's in charge of the prisoners, is negotiating with the opposite forces about possible letting go of the prisoners, and there's a whole separate command which is off, using his resources to take care of and liquidate the prisoners? I mean, that's the only scenario that I can figure out from what you're saying, and I'm really in a hard place trying to figure out how anybody could run an army like that. Maybe you could help me out.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, you're quite right. The situation was a very difficult one, very difficult. Negotiations. Now, the commander of the Zvornik Brigade was holding negotiations with commanders of the 28th Division, the representatives of the 28th Division, for opening up a corridor to let through the column which was moving from Srebrenica towards Tuzla, making this breakthrough. It was such a strong column that he didn't even dare resist it, stand up to it, because at the front itself with the 4th Battalion of the Zvornik Brigade, three trenches had been taken control of, and this was a dramatic operative situation in the area of responsibility of the Zvornik Brigade. The negotiations were not conducted to let the prisoners go. He did not have the mandate to do so. Therefore, the prisoners were not under his competence and authority, but probably he had the responsibility to be in charge of them and take care of them.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone please, Judge Wald.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: But he said in this very dispatch, one paragraph above, the negotiations, "If no one" -- "I can't take care of these problems," when he's referring to the large number of prisoners. He said, "If no one takes on the responsibility, I will be forced to let them go." He thought he had the authority to take care of the prisoners; at least, that's the way I read it, and to let them go.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. He had the responsibility, or rather, his people while he was at Zepa had the responsibility to be in charge of the prisoners, take care of them, but then following pursuant to orders from the Main Staff, the prisoners were taken over to the superior command. So the prisoners had to go to the collection centres, the holding areas, which the Republika Srpska had in the vicinity of -- in the northeast section, that is to say -- I can't think of the name of the place now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Batkovic?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't -- Batkovic, yes, thank you. Batkovic was the place. So it was a collection centre in Batkovici, and their responsibility was to that. But as that was not what was undertaken, he had to use up resources which he needed on the front, and that is why he is making this dramatic appeal. From the context of this, I can conclude that he did not know that those prisoners had been liquidated. Of course, that does not rid him of his responsibility, and I do not wish to do so. That's not what I'm trying to do. I don't want to justify him and rid him of the responsibility of the fact that that occurred in his area of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Cayley, I do apologise, but I myself have a question at this point. General, you are an expert witness, a military expert witness, a professional man. Now, imagine the following situation: You're the commander of a brigade, for example, and you reach the -- your various installations where the brigade is located, deployed, and you see that the Security Service, the Security Service has taken away the military police, the transport service, and other battalions, for example, to do something else that you don't know about. Now, what would you do, following military rules and regulations, faced with the situation like that? What would you do?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would first see where they had been taken to, and I would take steps. I would relieve them of their duties, bring them to task, and all the other measures and steps that I am authorised to take given a situation of that kind. But the commander of the brigade, on the 15th, returns from Zepa, and the first place he goes to is the command post and, from the operations duty officer, he asks for a situation report because he -- the circumstances are dramatic which brought him back to the zone of responsibility, and he has established a front at Zepa. So he has withdrawn the army, he's brought the units, and he's now seeking a situation report. He wants to know where the weakest points at the front towards Tuzla are, or rather, towards the column being withdrawn. So that is the problem which occupies him at that point. He focuses on that problem, how to close the void. And it is quite certain that he cannot deal with any other matters because he thought that the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. system, the police and security system, was seeing to those affairs. And from that situation, we received this information from him, this appeal. He is asking somebody else to be in charge of the prisoners, and it must be the superior command, the corps command -- or rather, the corps turns it over to the army of Republika Srpska and Batkovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, just one moment. When somebody informs the chief of the brigade with respect to the prisoners, don't you think that information, specific information about the prisoners should be imparted at this point?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course. Yes, of course. And I don't justify the system that did not give the proper information. But I'm just trying to explain why the Brigade Commander at that point did not know and could not have known, or to be more specific, need not have known, and that's how we come to get a report of this kind. That's why it's written in this way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Cayley, I apologise. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: I have just a small inquiry. You said that the Brigade Commander said that he would let them go and you inferred that they would be going to the collection centres or holding areas. He did not say that he was sending them there, did he? He just said, "I'll let them go," but he didn't say where.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the order or, rather, in the documents of the Command of the Drina Corps for Operation Srebrenica, and also in the document of the Main Staff of the army of Republika Srpska, it is prescribed how one should behave towards prisoners of war. So prisoners of war, by virtue of the document of the Main Staff, are put into the proper facilities and are handed over to the Superior Command. That was the duty, the responsibility. When the Brigade Commander returned from Zepa to the area of responsibility, he was told that the prisoners of war were in his area of responsibility, and he was asking why they weren't where they should have been pursuant to the order and that they were using up resources that he needed for the front. That's why he launched this appeal that he couldn't be in charge of the responsibilities, that somebody else had to look after them, which meant the Superior Command, and that if they did not take them over, he would be forced to let them go. So this is an appeal to the Superior Command to take over the prisoners of war. To our great misfortune and our shame, we know how they dealt with them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge Riad.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: General, we've already presented, put forward, that the 4th Battalion of the Zvornik, the military police of the Zvornik Brigade, and the engineers of the Zvornik were all engaged in Orahovac on the 14th of July in murdering people. Now, you're a military man. Put yourself in the position for one moment of Lieutenant Colonel Pandurevic returning to the brigade and the meeting that he had that you've discussed with the President with the operations officer. Now, do you not think that Colonel Pandurevic would have asked the operations officer, captain whoever, "Tell me, what has the 4th Brigade been -- what has the 4th Battalion been doing? What have the military police been doing? What have the engineers been doing?" Don't you think that Colonel Pandurevic would have asked those questions?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he knows exactly what the 4th Battalion was doing. It was holding the front. He knows what the battalion was doing. The question is whether somebody, whether anybody with parts of the 4th Battalion acted contrary to his orders because he gave orders where the 4th Battalion was to be. But quite obviously, somebody used the 4th Battalion for different purposes, and that 4th Battalion had the most difficult situation at the front and that is where the corridor was, in fact, opened up for the column to move through because the 4th Battalion had lost its positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: What do you think the operations officer said to Colonel Pandurevic about this robbed part of the 4th Battalion and the military police and the engineers? What do you think he told Colonel Pandurevic about what they'd been doing in Orahovac?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The operations officer told the Brigade Commander, gave him as a -- brought him up-to-date with the situation on the front. That was the urgent information which the commander was exclusively interested in at the beginning, as soon as he arrived, to understand the situation facing his brigade. After that, he learnt -- somebody told him that there were prisoners of war in his area of responsibility and probably he was told the localities. He does not specify the localities. Whether he knew them or not, I can't say, but I allow for the possibility that he knew the localities as well. And he was informed that his people were there engaged in security. But I'm quite certain that nobody told him his 4th Battalion was busy murdering prisoners of war. I'm quite convinced of that, because he wouldn't have written an information of this kind. He wouldn't have written a report of this kind. He would have written quite a different report.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: General, let's go back to the order and the sort of key paragraph. "An additional burden for us is the large number of prisoners distributed throughout schools in the brigade area, as well as obligations of security and restoration of the terrain." I want to concentrate on the word "security" for a moment. Who was the assistant commander for security in the Drina Corps?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The assistant commander for security, I believe, was Nikolic, for security. Please help me if I can't remember his first name.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: It's -- the name is Lieutenant Colonel Popovic, Nikolic --

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, that's in the corps, sir. That's in the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: That's the question I asked you. You must have got a misinterpretation.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understood you to be asking about the Zvornik Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: So we're agreed that the assistant commander for security in the Drina Corps was Lieutenant Colonel Popovic.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Who was the security officer, the chief of security, in the Main Staff of the VRS?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The chief of security in the Main Staff of the VRS was Beara.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: So we're agreed it was Colonel Ljubo Beara.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, General, you're aware that it is the Prosecutor's position that Colonel Popovic and Colonel Beara were involved in the murder of thousands of Muslim prisoners in the Zvornik area? Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the documents which I studied, I did not come across that kind of information nor did I glean it. But in reading some intercepts, that kind of information is contained there, although I have my reservations with respect to that material. But I am aware of the fact which is contained in those conversations.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, General, bearing in mind that Colonel Pandurevic is using the word "security," you would agree with me that what he is referring to is the murder of thousands of Muslims by Colonel Popovic and Colonel Beara? That's what he's referring to in this report, isn't he, General?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this report? No.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: General --

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this report -- please, sir. This report says, the last sentence, "As well as obligations of security." "Obezbedjenje" means "control," "supervision," and so on, and that implies -- that is what we mean by the word in my language of "obezbedjenje."

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: General, the word --

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not "bezbednost."

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: General, the word "restoration," can you explain to the Judges what that means in military terminology?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Clearing up of the battlefield is an action which is undertaken in order to -- that in the area where there was fighting to clear up the consequences of that fighting, and that means picking up the casualties, both human and animal, and burying the bodies and usually the animal remains are burnt. "Clearing up" means also control of drinking water. It also implies taking control of the epidemiological situation, to avoid any disease, epidemics from spreading. So that is the term that "clearing up" means. It means to undertake all the necessary measures which would enable an area which -- upon which combat had taken place should be brought into a proper state. That is what we mean by clearing up the battlefield. It implies a whole complex of steps and measures and also means the taking of hygienic and technical measures with respect to people in the area -- people who spent time in the area, once again to prevent epidemics and so on and so forth. So that is what we mean in broad terms by clearing up the battlefield.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, General, I have the military lexicon in front of me of the JNA. I'm not going to waste time showing it to you, but what I'm particularly interested in is the meaning -- you've stated it yourself, that "asanacija" means burying the dead, doesn't it General? That is one of the meanings of the term "asanacija."

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is one of the acts undertaken within the framework of the asanacija procedures.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And indeed when Colonel Pandurevic is referring to restoration in this report, General, he's referring to burying thousands of dead Muslims who have been executed. That's what he's talking about, isn't he, General? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I do not make such a conclusion. Asanacija of the battlefield is something that the operations commander has to address in coordination with the Civil Defence, the medical corps, and so on. Bodies found are buried as part of that procedure, but restoration of the terrain or asanacija cannot be identified with what you are implying.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, General, fighting in the Zvornik area, as you know, did not cease until the 17th of July of 1995, did it?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was fighting even later, but on the 17th of July, the corridor was closed. Most of the column had passed through, but there were battles later on as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: So are you suggesting to the Court that Colonel Pandurevic was busily clearing up the battlefield with ongoing fighting against Muslims in the area? Is that what you're suggesting? On the 15th of July, with ongoing fighting, he's wandering the battlefield with his units, clearing it up. Is that what you're suggesting?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, this is a document dated the 15th, the 15th, and of course Pandurevic is not doing asanacija on the 15th, but a part of the resources of the brigade have to be engaged for that too.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: General, Colonel Pandurevic is reporting on the 15th of July that one of the burdens that he has is the restoration of the terrain, and you and I both know it's a fact that he was not clearing the battlefield on the 15th of July. He's talking about burying the bodies of executed Muslims, isn't he, General?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If that was the action he was engaged in exclusively, he would call it that. He wouldn't say "restoration of the terrain," he would say "burial of killed prisoners." However, as he's talking about restoration of the terrain, I am prone to interpret it as activities which involve all the actions that I have described.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. President -- I'm sorry, Judge Riad.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: General, would such things as burying the killed prisoners be openly stated in reports or in correspondence? I think I understood that differently, that these things are not to be said openly. I think I even heard you saying that.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They are not said openly. But if the report really did refer to liquidation of people, then there was no need to conceal it because if everyone in the communications chain knew about it, then there would be no need to hide it behind the term "asanacija," which implies much more than burial. It also implies finding the casualties, collecting them in particular places, and taking all the other measures, as I have no other possibilities of interpreting this term in any other way but to include all these other activities. It certainly does not imply only that, but once the commander finds out, then the term covers that, too. But I think, and I'm almost sure, that at the time this report was compiled, he was not aware that he had this problem, too, in his area of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Cayley.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Do you wish to take a pause now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, perhaps this would be a good time. I should like to take advantage of the opportunity to give you some good news, Mr. Cayley, that you have acquired 23 additional minutes. This is the time the Judges took away from you. So we're going to have a 20-minute break.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I'll be finished soon, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Cayley, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. If the General could be provided with Prosecutor's Exhibit 614, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: General, this is an interim combat report from Lieutenant Colonel Pandurevic from the 16th of July of 1995. Are you familiar with this document? Have you seen this before?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I'm particularly interested in the final paragraph, the paragraph 6. After you've read that -- do you have paragraph 6 there? Could you read out the final sentence of paragraph 6, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Mr. Cayley, take care of the throat of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I was thinking of my throat, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Yes, okay. We have to balance these things.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I'll read it, General, in order to save your vocal chords. "I consider that the Krivaja 95 operation is not complete as long as a single enemy soldier or civilian remains behind the front line." Now, General, you know that by the 16th of July of 1995, the movement of the civilian population from Srebrenica was complete, wasn't it? In fact, it was completed on the 13th of July of 1995, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 13th in the evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: So by that time, these 30.000 civilians had left the enclave and were now on Muslim-controlled territory?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is what follows from the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And also by the 16th of July, you're aware that there had been executions in the Jadar River, Cerska Valley, Kravica, Orahovac, the dam at Petkovci, Branjevo farm, the Pilica school, the Pilica Dom, and Kozluk. You are aware that there had been -- of the executions that we know about, they had all taken place by the 16th of July, hadn't they, General?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Everything in connection with the locations, the dynamics, and the dates of the executions contained in Mr. Butler's testimony is something I agree with. I have studied it in detail, and I concur.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: So by the 16th of July, General, in essence, the Muslim community in Srebrenica had been extinguished apart from the stragglers that were left in Zvornik; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't say extinguished or destroyed. According to the documents, about 30.000 people were relocated, and by the 13th of the evening, they were in territory under the control of the Muslim army and authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: By the 16th of July, General, apart from the stragglers in Zvornik, the population, including the male members, were either moved to Tuzla, or they were dead. That's right, isn't it, General?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were moved to Tuzla, plus the information on the executions that I have studied and with which I concur.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And that's exactly what Colonel Pandurevic is talking about in this document, isn't he? He's saying that Krivaja 95 is not complete until every single member of the Muslim army or civilians are either moved or dead. That's what he's saying, isn't he, General?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you really think that a brigade commander can rule when an operation is over? An operation is over when the aims set in the order of the Corps Commander have been attained, and that is capturing the prominent features around Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: General --

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The operation was completed on the 11th.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: -- that is not what the brigade commander is saying. The brigade commander is saying that, "Krivaja 95 is not complete as long as a single enemy soldier or civilian remains behind the front line." And by that, he's saying, "Krivaja 95 is not complete until all of the civilians have been moved and we've killed all the Muslim soldiers." That's what he's saying, isn't he, General?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he's not saying that. First of all, he doesn't know whether the operation has been completed or not. The person who planned and executed the operation knows that, and his superior commander, the commander of the Drina Corps, or rather, the Drina Corps command, and the Main Staff command. The commander of the Zvornik Brigade was only one of the participants in the operation, and in a limited manner. And as of the 12th, he is already near Srebrenica and he certainly does not know when the operation was completed. Other people know that. His statement I interpret as meaning that he believes that some of the consequences of that operation, such as the capturing of prisoners of war and their settlement in his area of responsibility, is a consequence of the operation. That is his interpretation. It doesn't mean that he's right. It does not mean that the operation is not completed. The operation was completed on the 11th.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: So your evidence is that one of the brigade commanders of the Drina Corps had a completely different understanding of the purpose of Krivaja 95 as compared to everybody else in the Drina Corps headquarters and all of the other brigade commanders. Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I'm saying is that the Commander of the Zvornik Brigade did not consider the aim of the operation to be the destruction of the last remaining Muslim. The aim of the operation is determined by the corps commander, and he defined it in his order for active combat.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If we could have Prosecutor's Exhibit 675, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, General, this is an order that you've already referred to in your evidence, and, in particular, you referred to paragraph 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: So, Mr. Usher, if page 2 could be placed on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And Lieutenant Colonel Pandurevic writes, on the 18th of July: "During the last 10 days or so the municipality of Zvornik has been swamped with Srebrenica Turks." "Derogatory term for the Muslims" is the translator's note. "It is inconceivable to me that someone brought in 3.000 Turks of military age and placed them in schools in the municipality, in addition to the 7.000 or so who have fled into the forests. This has created an extremely complex situation and the possibility of the total occupation of Zvornik in conjunction with the forces at the front. These actions have stirred up great discontent among the people and the general opinion is that Zvornik is to pay the price for the taking of Srebrenica." Now, General, you would agree with me that by the 18th of July, apart from the execution at Nezluk, all of the prisoners within the Zvornik area of command have been executed, have they not?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: So by that time, you would agree with me that Lieutenant Colonel Pandurevic, even if on your theory he didn't know on the 15th of July that thousands of Muslims had been killed in Zvornik, he certainly knew that a lot of Muslim prisoners had been killed in his area of responsibility by the 18th of July of 1995, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From this paragraph on page 3, that is, point 4, it is indeed possible to infer that the Commander of the Zvornik Brigade is aware of the executions in his zone, but also he says explicitly that he cannot understand that someone should have brought 3.000 military-aged Turks, as he says, and puts them in schools in the municipality. So he says somebody, somebody else brought them there.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And when he states that "these actions have stirred up great discontent among the people and the general opinion is that Zvornik is to pay the price for the taking of Srebrenica," what he's saying to the Drina Corps Command is that there's a great deal of discontent in Zvornik because everybody in Zvornik knows that thousands of Muslims have been killed in the Zvornik area. That's what he's saying, isn't he, General?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, that too can be inferred from the contents of this paragraph, but he's also thinking of the 7.000 who had fled and who could link up with the 2nd Corps and lead to the fall of Zvornik, but he does have what you are saying in mind as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: He's angry, isn't he, General, because his whole area is soaked in Muslim blood. That's what he's saying to the Drina Corps. The population, the Serbian population was discontented with that situation, weren't they, General?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The Brigade Commander, who probably learnt what had happened, is furious that this had happened and that somebody did it without his knowing about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: We can move on, Mr. President, to another area, and I'm gradually getting to the end. If the following exhibits could be made available: Prosecutor's Exhibit 435 and Defence Exhibit 151. If 151 could be placed onto -- Defence 151. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, General, my understanding of your testimony was that within the Drina Corps, the Chief of Staff had no command authority over the assistant commanders. He only had command authority over his own staff; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And if the witness could be shown, please, Prosecutor's Exhibit 435.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, General, on the 12th of July, General Krstic was the Chief of Staff of the brigade, wasn't he? Of the corps, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of the corps, yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, this is an intercept that you have seen before, and in it, General Krstic is giving orders to Lieutenant Colonel Krsmanovic, the Chief of Transport of the Drina Corps. Now, since Colonel Krsmanovic was directly underneath the assistant commander for rear services, under your theory, General Krstic should have had no authority to give this man orders, should he?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In principle, I have reservations towards intercepts, as a matter of principle, and I can back this up with arguments. If I may be allowed, I can tell you what I think about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: General. General.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will answer your question. I will answer your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Let us say this is a hypothetical situation. For one moment, put your reservations about the intercepts to one side. Mr. Visnjic can deal with that in his re-examination. If this is correct, if General Krstic is, in fact, giving an order to Lieutenant Colonel Krsmanovic, then your theory that the Chief of Staff has no authority over assistant commanders or their subordinates is incorrect, isn't it, General?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. My theory is correct. But you have to bear in mind another fact and that is that General Krstic is also the deputy commander, and whenever the corps commander is not able to issue an order or is physically not present or is away somewhere and a commander, a subordinate commander requires explanations, the Chief of Staff, as the deputy corps commander, has the authority to issue an order on behalf of the commander. And if such a situation were to arise, as reflected in this intercept, General Krstic would have full authority to order the assistant for rear services because the Corps Commander has already issued such an order. So he's acting pursuant to the order of the Corps Commander or on the basis of his oral decision. We don't know the background, the context of this order. Whether he had authority to do that or not, we would be able to say only if we knew where the Corps Commander was at that point in time, where General Krstic was, and where this officer Krsmanovic was. And without knowing that, it is very difficult to answer your question. I have said as a rule that the Chief of Staff of the Corps as the Deputy Commander is authorised to issue orders when the commander is unable to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And he's authorised to issue those orders to assistant commanders and brigades when the commander is not available to issue those orders himself, isn't he, General?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If we could now move on. General, I want to discuss with you a little the rules of service of the security organ which you discussed in the, I think, the final day of your examination-in-chief. And you stated that paragraph 49 of those rules, which deals with secret information, essentially creates a fissure or crack within the command structure of military units of the VRS. Do you recall your fissure or crack theory?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now if, please, Prosecutor's Exhibit 418 could be made available.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, General, do you recall stating that prisoners of war are essentially the responsibility of the assistant commander --

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't hear that, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Do you recall stating in your evidence that prisoners of war are the responsibility of the security section, the assistant commander for security, and also the chief of intelligence or the intelligence body of the corps? Do you recall stating that?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Everything within the unit is the commander's responsibility, but for certain departments, he has his assistants, and therefore the security department covers the treatment of prisoners of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Let me read to you your evidence, General, and this is on page 8064. "In the system of command of the prisoners of war, by nature of this duty, it would have to be the security organs and intelligence organs who would deal with this, but first and foremost the security organs." Now, based on what you said, General, would I be right in concluding that both the intelligence organ and the security organ were involved in dealing with prisoners of war?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, only the security organs. The intelligence organs provide information for the Security Service when interrogating prisoners of war, Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. information about the enemy. So they are only users of information about the enemy side obtained through the interrogation of prisoners of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, General, if you could --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: General, if you could look at paragraph 16, and I will read this: "The security organ is directly subordinate to the commanding officer of the command, unit, institution, or staff of the armed forces in whose strength it is placed in the establishment, and it is responsible to that officer for its work, while JNA security organs," and then it goes on to talk about the federal secretary for national defence. Now, General, who was the assistant commander for security in the Drina Corps?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Lieutenant Colonel Popovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, if we substitute Lieutenant Colonel Popovic's name in place of "security organ," it reads, this document, "Lieutenant Colonel Popovic is directly subordinate to the commanding officer of the command, unit, institution, or staff of the armed forces in whose strength it is placed in the establishment ..." Now, General, since Colonel Popovic was the assistant commander for security within the Drina Corps, on the basis of that regulation, he was directly subordinate, was he not, to the commander of the Drina Corps; that is who he answered to?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the commander of the Drina Corps, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, going back to your fissure or crack theory, I wish to read to you, and if the witness can be shown Prosecutor's Exhibit 399 -- so bear in mind the theory that you put forward that there was, in fact, a fissure in the command chain. I can read this to you if there's a problem in finding it. This is General Krstic's interview, and this is what he stated.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: On page 61 in the English and on page 37, Mr. Visnjic, in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: "I cannot be responsible for the acts of Lieutenant Colonel Popovic because he's an individual. In all this, he was activated by the order of General Mladic and the chief of security administration going along the line of the chain of command of security." General, based on your crack theory, was Lieutenant Colonel Popovic -- were Lieutenant Colonel Popovic and Colonel Beara and General Mladic the individuals responsible for killing thousands of Muslim prisoners of war?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot answer your question whether they are responsible for the killing of Muslims or not. I can talk about the role of the Security Service in the system of command, and about the possible crack in the command system which resulted in the independence of the Security Service, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: General, these were the security officers in the Drina Corps and the Main Staff, and General Mladic was in command of the entire VRS. These are the very people. Were these the people, General, who were responsible, Colonel Beara and Colonel Popovic; were they responsible for killing all these people?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I should like to object to the question of my learned friend Mr. Cayley. It is the submission of the Defence that this question belongs to a certain investigation engaged in by the Prosecution, and I don't see how the witness can, within the context of his answers, determine whether somebody is responsible or not when he did not address that issue, as the witness has told us several times. If the Prosecution wishes to investigate, I would appeal that he refrains from doing so in his questions to this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Cayley, do you wish to respond?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, the witness, an expert, has put forward a theory to the Court that there was a crack in the command chain, and he's essentially inferred, said expressly, that this security organ was working all by itself. Now, we know who the individuals are that were in the security branch. Now, if he's putting that theory forward, he can certainly make that theory good by actually inserting the actors into his theory and telling the Court whether or not his investigation indicates that these people are responsible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I think that Mr. Cayley has provided the answer himself. If the witness has presented a certain theory and the Prosecution knows who the people are holding certain functions, I don't see why we should insist on this question, especially as the witness cannot give the answer as to what the function of those people were at that moment. He has said repeatedly that he has not studied those individuals in particular, whether they were there at the time, whether they knew about it or not, and so on and so forth. So this process of drawing conclusions is up to the Prosecution, not the witness. A further point, Mr. President - I apologise - I thought that the subject of this examination was the responsibility of General Krstic and not the possible responsibility of other people involved. The question is whether General Krstic is responsible or not and not whether somebody else is responsible or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Cayley, bearing in mind the fact that we have a military expert witness, you perhaps could rephrase your question without using the term "responsible" because, after all, that is a judicial term. So could you rephrase your questions, perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
