utterances.text: When you say something is wrong with microphone, we hear, so --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The General said, "Until the moment when they shake hands, the former, the outgoing commander, is in command." And the moment when they're shaking hands, he doesn't really know who is, that very moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: At that moment, would the decree decide, the presidential decree decide?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The presidential decree prescribes, orders, on what date, as the earliest date, the new commander may take over duty and the former commander give up his duty. It cannot be done before that day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness be shown Exhibit 403, 760; and could the English version be placed on the ELMO, please. And for the transcript, 403. That is the number of the OTP exhibit. Paragraph 7.60.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Have you found it?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: As I know you have a problem with your throat, let me read it: "While he did not formally relinquish command of the brigade when he assumed command of the `tactical group' deployed to Srebrenica, he left the daily operations of the brigade in the hands of his Chief of Staff, Brigade Deputy Commander, Major Dragan Obrenovic." General Radinovic, this is analysis by the Prosecution expert witness Mr. Butler. In formal terms, in any document was a tactical group appointed which was led by the Commander of the Zvornik Brigade?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you referring to Krivaja 95?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Yes, I'm referring to Krivaja 95. As we can see from this paragraph, the period is from the 2nd to the 4th and onwards.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That phrase was not used for a part of the forces of the Zvornik Brigade that were engaged in the operation Krivaja 95.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Did the Commander of the Zvornik Brigade issue any kind of document with the words "tactical group" in the heading?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I have not seen any such document.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Did Major-General -- was Major-General Radislav Krstic commander of the operative group for Zepa?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Did Major-General Radislav Krstic issue any document with the indication in the heading "Operative Group"?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: The allegation by the Prosecution expert witness Mr. Butler, does it completely coincide with your own submission? Only we're talking about tactical groups here as opposed to operational group, which are different in size, but in terms of formal command and documents issued by those groups.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Regarding this assertion, Mr. Butler as the Prosecution witness and myself are fully in agreement. He claims that Lieutenant Colonel Vinko Pandurevic was commander of the Tactical Group for Krivaja 95, even though he was not formally called that, just as I am claiming that General Radislav Krstic was commander of the operative group for the Zepa operation, even though it was not called that in formal terms. But more important than the formal name is the actual state of affairs. Indeed, they were forces that were, in terms of strength, area, method of combat, an operative group, and that is why I have used that phrase.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I should like to ask that the witness be shown Prosecution Exhibit 675 now, please. Could we see point 4 on the ELMO, please. Could you focus on point 4 of this report. It is an interim combat report of the Zvornik Brigade, dated the 18th of July, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General Radinovic, you answered questions put to you by the Prosecution with respect to this document and this particular paragraph. I should just like to ask you to explain to the Trial Chamber part of this report, that portion in which Colonel Pandurevic says that someone brought the prisoners, military-able Turks, and distributed them around the municipality. What does that mean, "someone"? From this paragraph, "someone brought."

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From this paragraph, we arrive at the incontestable conclusion that the Commander of the Zvornik Brigade, at the time when he issued this document, knew that in his zone of responsibility in the last ten days there were prisoners of war, and he sets a figure, that they were there. He says that someone brought in -- brought them in, that someone brought them in, that the command system of the Drina Corps -- if the command system of the Drina Corps, Vinko Pandurevic as Commander of the Zvornik Brigade, would have been informed of that through the chain of command, and he would not send out a report to the Corps Command in the form of a protest, because this is a protest. We have here a protest over the fact that someone had brought in these prisoners of war to his zone of responsibility. That means that he did not do so nor did he do so pursuant to a command, an order. What is worst and what is most tragic and worst of all, we can see that from the sentence, the last sentence, in fact. We can really -- we understand that he knows what was done with them because there is a great lot of dissatisfaction amongst the people with this kind of conduct, probably thinking about the liquidation of the prisoners of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General Radinovic, as my learned colleague Mr. Cayley on several occasions intimated this, let me ask you in the end what is your view of the intercepted conversations, the intercepts, as probative value, taking -- on the basis of your research? What would you have to say?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I owe the Trial Chamber an explanation, and the Prosecution as well, why I did not use the intercepts as evidence and empirical background and basis for arriving at my own conclusions despite the fact that I studied them all, and let me say I studied them in depth. I will present my reasons and it will be up to the Trial Chamber to assess whether I was right or wrong. I just had the transcripts in my possession. I did not have the audiotapes, audio recordings, so I was not able to ascertain whether what was written down was actually said. Second, in many places in those intercepts I was not able to ascertain the identity of the speaker -- the speakers, the colloquiters [sic]. Third, it was impossible for me to follow the context in which the conversation took place and, first of all, I have in mind of the operative -- operational context for me to have a full knowledge of the situation and thus to be able to possibly evaluate what was contained in those intercepts. And the most important argument for me why I did not use and could not use those conversations, those intercepts as an argument in drawing my conclusions was the fact that, in preparation for this trial, I did not come across the fact that a so-called primary interpretation of the conversation had been carried out. And for me to be able to use those intercepts as evidence and proof, I want to have myself been able to conduct that primary interpretation. In view of all the foregoing, of everything I have said so far, these restrictions and limitations, I did not have this primary interpretation. I was not able to conduct a primary interpretation. Now, what do I mean when I say that? The conversations would have had to be put in two statistical series, that means series on the basis of theme and subject matter; second, their dynamics, that is to say, time, time period, give a time frame; and the origins, who the speakers are. According to hierarchical structure in the system of command and by virtue of belonging to command systems, that is to say, the Main Staff, the Drina Corps, the Drina Corps, the brigades, all these relationships, one brigade to another brigade, the MUP, the operative command, parallel participants within the staff structures, therefore, I was lacking in this background. I did not have a primary interpretation of the facts for me to be able to prepare them for analysis and the drawing of conclusions. For that type of work, I did not even have the elementary prerequisites, which means that I was not able to undertake all the preliminary steps, studying authenticity, ascertaining authenticity, a time frame, the subject matter, and so on. I was not able to do that, and so I had to leave them out of my registry of basic conversations. And they would have, of course, been welcome had they been properly prepared for a proper analysis. But this would require extremely extensive preparatory work which was not done for this particular occasion and for this particular purpose.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General Radinovic, you said that in the course of your research you talked to General Zivanovic. When was that?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't give you an exact date. I don't know that. But it was snowing. There was snow and it was -- that means it was February and March, which is the snow period in the country.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: You mean the year 2000?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, 2000.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: At that time, how many documents did you have, including the Defence documents and the documents disclosed by the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, unfortunately, at that time, I did not have very many documents, the ones that I call primary source of data and information, that is to say, the operational documents, operative documents. And if I were to measure that in proportion compared to what I have now, it would just be a fifth, a fifth of the documents that I have now. The studies that I used, I had almost all the studies except Carl Bildt's book, which came out later on, so I did have the books.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: When did you receive the bulk of the material, most of the documents? When was that?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I received the bulk of the documents for preparing my findings and for my own personal preparations, I received the bulk sometime in June, July, which I think coincides with the time, and let me be quite frank and say that an invaluable contribution was the brilliant expert report by Mr. Butler. It was a role model, and he must have had enormous help from a series of assistants, each of whom did his work very well in order to be able to come up with that kind of report.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have asked the General these questions -- let me just remind you that most of the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. documents were disclosed by the Prosecution in keeping with the rules and regulations, but it was only prior to the testimony of Mr. Butler, actually. I say that just by way of information to you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: And my last question, General Radinovic: If we look at that whole period of time from the beginning of the Srebrenica operation up until the end of the operation for Zepa, at which points did the command composition of the Main Staff interfere with the system of command of the Drina Corps?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The command system of the Main Staff, in keeping with its authorisations and competencies, interfered with the Drina Corps command in several ways, modalities, and points, points in the sense of dynamics, and in space, the operations of the Drina Corps. The Main Staff did this with the help of acts of command, orders via its -- through its authorised representatives. In the documents, we can see that on different occasions, in different localities, the representatives of the Main Staff would arrive and become involved in the command posts and the process of decision-making in the Drina Corps of the forward command post at Pribicevac -- from the forward command post at Pribicevac further on. However, there were decisions which directly either disenfranchised or directly compelled the command of the Drina Corps, and I think that that is meritorious for an assessment of the situation that we are discussing here. The first radical decision --

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Just a moment. For purposes of the record, you said disempowered or directly committed, disempowered or directly committed?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Both, I said both. The first radical obligation, duty of the Drina Corps, on the basis of direct interference of the Main Staff relates to an expansion of the goals of the Operation Krivaja 95, as we have heard here on several occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General Radinovic, if that is not a problem, as we've already heard a lot about each of these subjects, could you just give us a brief review of what those points were.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, an expansion of the goals of the Operation Krivaja 95, which meant the taking control of Srebrenica. The second radical form of inclusion by the Main Staff into the system of command of the Drina Corps was the realisation and leading of the population -- of moving out the population from the UNPROFOR base at Potocari. The third instance was the order and assigning the mandate to General Krstic and the Drina Corps to launch the Zepa operation and implement it. And finally, fourth, the direct disempowerment of the command of the Drina Corps, and that was the order dated the 17th of July pertaining to the formation of a provisional command led by the officer of the Main Staff of the VRS, Lieutenant Colonel Keserovic, for joining up the activities, linking up the activities in the Bratunac-Drinjaca-Milici zone to search the terrain. There was the Milici Brigade there, the Bratunac Brigade, the 65th Protection Regiment, and I think parts of the 67th Regiment as well, and other units which found themselves there, along with an unexplained, insufficiently known to me, role of the command system of the Main Staff and individual elements of the security and police system with respect to the prisoners of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General Radinovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Just to repeat what you are saying; all this would still be under the command and the control of the commander of the Drina Corps, or would it be a parallel, completely parallel line?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, in this chain of events which I have enumerated, there were decrees which completely excluded the Drina Corps as a command in charge and at the head of the operation. The command of the Drina Corps did not -- was not in charge of the operation to move out the population. It was the Main Staff that was in charge of that operation. Second, the Main Staff directly conjoined all the activities of the forces engaged in searching the terrain from the 17th to the 19th of July. So those are two episodes where the Main Staff really and actually disempowered the command of the Drina Corps. The other forms of interference that I spoke about earlier on were decisions which were binding on the command of the Drina Corps which obliged it to behave pursuant to the orders given, i.e., to expand the goals of the operation and to launch a new operation on Zepa, which had a vital effect on the whole command system of the Drina Corps in that whole post-operative situation after Krivaja 95.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see that Mr. Visnjic has completed his re-examination. Before we go on to the Judges' questions, perhaps we should have a ten-minute break. So we'll now have a ten-minute break and come back for the questions of the Judges.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge Riad.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I have no questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. Madam Judge Wald, if you please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Thank you. I want to open, Professor, by thanking you to come to testify before us. I think your overview will be of great assistance to us in the final analysis, but there are about seven or eight questions I have, and I hope that we can get through them in the next 20 minutes or so. The first one is that I believe you testified that if a VRS officer were to receive an order that he recognised as violating law, either his own law or international law, that his duty would be not to execute it, to try to get it in writing, not to execute it, and to tell the superior, as it were. Now, what I would like you to answer for me is what we call a hypothetical, and I'm sure you're familiar with a hypothetical, and that is suppose that a law -- an order which was clearly recognised by the officer receiving it as violating international law came from the Commander-in-Chief of the army, of the entire army, what would be the recourse of the officer who received that? This is a hypothetical. Under your view of both the law in effect at that time for VRS officers and international law. Does he have any recourse?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, in the rules governing the execution of orders, there's an explicit prohibition not to execute orders which violate the law. Now, this concept of violation of the law, as a non-expert, I take the liberty of saying that it is very broad. It can be interpreted in a variety of ways, from mildest violations to war crimes. That is not my speciality, and I won't go into it. But what recourse does a soldier or officer or general or commander have who receives an order, the execution of which would imply a violation of the law? Every officer is duty-bound to caution the person giving him that order that that order is contrary to the law and contrary to the rules that apply for that profession. The superior is duty-bound or, rather, it is his right to respond or turn a deaf ear, but he must suffer the consequences. The subordinate must not execute an order which implies a violation of the law. There is nothing that can justify him. The execution of laws which violate -- the execution of orders which violate the law imply consequences for the person giving the order and for the person executing the order. The principles are quite clear in that respect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Does the officer, and you covered this in your testimony as well, I believe, does the officer who sees a violation of law, a clear -- let's posit a clear violation of law, no question in his mind. When he sees that being committed by another officer in the same army, perhaps not even the same level of command or the same brigade or battalion, but when he sees that being violated by another officer even though he is not the recipient of the direct command himself, does he have a duty to report that violation to someone?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He does.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: And I will go back to my original question. Suppose that hypothetically, suppose that the violation comes from the highest levels of the command in the army, does he have an obligation to go above the army into the civilian commander-in-chief, perhaps the president of the company? Does he have some duty to go above the highest command if it is the highest command that is doing the violating?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He does have that obligation, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: I appreciate your answer very much. Now let me go on to the second question. You said at one point -- this is a -- more of a strategic tactical question drawing upon your experience, both as a theoretician in military matters and your practical experience in the army. I think you said at one point that control of Srebrenica was considered to be a "to be or not to be" situation in the Serbian objectives in 1995 of having contiguous territory in which Serb populations could live. My question would be, why would -- if that is true, why would the VRS have been content to keep to the borders and to restrict them a little bit, the territory of the enclave, and to try to prevent communication between the enclaves of Srebrenica and Zepa, as you outline and we've heard outlined by others, the original objectives for Krivaja 95, why would they have thought that an adequate solution to the problem that had been persisting, in their view, from years and years, that that wouldn't deteriorate quickly back into the old situation where these enclaves would become, in their view, the centre for activities, guerilla-like activities, communication back and forth, and they would be right back where they were to begin with? Why would the more useful, utilitarian objective not be to get control of the territory? I'm not now talking about doing it by illegal means, but to, in other words, to get the people out of there and get control of the territory? What was useful to them beyond the immediate in the original objectives of Krivaja 95?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When the Drina Corps command was assigned the task of executing Krivaja 95, and when this was defined in the order for active combat for Krivaja 95, the limited objectives were indicated. The most important military operational goal then was to prevent military activity by forces of the 28th Division from the enclaves towards the VRS which held the front line around the enclaves. So that was the logic behind the determination of the military objective. Why? I do not consider it to have been productive, in military or political terms, to set as a goal the capture of Srebrenica, and I think a similar analysis was made by the army of Republika Srpska in 1995, and that is that these were safe areas protected by the United Nations. And a radical goal, that is, capturing the whole area fully, was incumbent with the risk of clashing with the United Nations mechanism which was, of course, not in the strategic interest of Republika Srpska or its army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Okay, thank you.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And there's one further point, if I may make, in response to your question. It was quite clear that whatever the outcome of the war in accordance with the objectives that I presented them or some objectives as seen by others, but peace had to come to Bosnia-Herzegovina eventually, and this means that there was absolutely no possibility of any territory -- any part of Bosnia-Herzegovina remaining ethnically pure. Cohabitation had to be re-established, and any violence which involved violence towards the civilian population postponed that peace for a long time. And I assure you that in 1995, and much before that, but in 1995 certainly it was the greatest interest of the Serb people everywhere, and especially in that part of Republika Srpska, to have peace restored as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Okay. You testified, I believe, that you concluded that Krivaja 95, and we've just talked about this, was never intended originally to capture, we just talked about that, Srebrenica; but of course, as you -- your report shows and the others, General Mladic did change the objective in midstream, as it were, and he extended the objectives of Krivaja 95 to cover -- or, at least, he went ahead to order the capture of Srebrenica. And indeed, he was on his way to extending that down to Bratunac and Zvornik, but his Generals, including General Krstic, prevailed upon him not to do that for many of the same reasons you've just detailed. My question is: If indeed all of the necessary rules and regulations and papers and documents that usually accompany the implementation of a formal plan such as Krivaja 95 could be, in effect, dispensed with, dispatched with, overruled by the on-the-spot decision of the single person in command, why couldn't that have been equally true about many of the other points of decision that you said could not happen because the rules and regulations wouldn't permit them, such as the change of the date of General Krstic's appointment to be earlier than the effective date on the document or some of the objectives of the evacuation? Why are we to believe that, in fact, there was a general, a general tenor of following the rules and regulations when we have such dramatic instances before us where they were completely thrown to the side on the on-the-spot decision of the Commander-in-Chief of the entire army?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, this is a hypothetical but also a practical question. It is hypothetical in the sense that whether that is possible in principle. The senior commanders, in this particular case the Commander of the Main Staff, has the power to extend goals and objectives. It is not in the power of the subordinate to check the correctness of the commander's ideas regarding the conduct of the operation, on condition that it is militarily legitimately executed. They have an obligation to draw his attention to all the negative consequences, but his is the last word, except, of course, regarding decisions which, as you said in your question, are flagrant violations of the law and conventions. This particular case and this example and this right also applies to the appointments by the Supreme Commander and no one may, in his name or sidestepping him, appoint a commander to a command position. In the course of the execution of decisions, a decision may be corrected if that proves to be necessary or if it is judged that a correction would be productive from the strategic point of view. Of course, it is only eventually that that assessment can be verified. But decision on appointment cannot be changed. A decree on appointment cannot be changed by anyone's decision except by the person who issued that decision or that decree, and nothing may be changed in the structure of the decree without the knowledge and consent of the person issuing it. I don't know whether my answer's satisfactory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Yes. You've answered my question. Thank you. My next one is that you said at one point that, unlike the situation in some other armies, the Main Staff in the VRS had some command responsibility. I think that's correct. Now, my question is: Is it your understanding that Main Staffers or people who are officers of the Main Staff had the power to requisition the assets and the personnel of corps such as the Drina Corps for their own purposes? They did have the power. In other words, a Main Staffer - again you can call it hypothetical if you want but I think you've discussed the possibility yourself - a Main Staffer could go to one of the brigades in the Drina Corps and say, "I want some equipment, I want some personnel to do something that's part of my Main Staff responsibility," and at that point the Drina Corps personnel would have to accede? I mean, assuming his level was high enough. And if so, did they even have to report that to their own command or they just took the men and the equipment and went with him without leaving any records or report behind to their own command structure? How did that work?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In principle, the senior command does have the power to use the resources of a lower-level command. In this particular case, the Main Staff of the VRS does not have any army of its own. It only has the army of Republika Srpska, which means in the areas of responsibilities it has its corps and it has some units that were under their direct command, like the 65th Protection Regiment, the 67th Communications Regiment, the 10th Diversionary Detachment, and so on. So if the Main Staff plans an operation and executes an operation, it cannot do so without relying on the resources on the ground, and in that sense, I don't think there is nothing in dispute. But --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: My question, if I can interrupt you, would be how that's done. In other words, assume exactly what you said, that the Main Staff has an operation. It needs some of the assets, both personnel and equipment, of one of the brigades. Now, does it just go in itself -- say it's a high enough person, an Assistant Commander from the Main Staff. Does he just go and say, "I'm ordering you to give me your equipment," or does he have to go through the top levels of the brigade, go to the Brigade Commander and say, "I want so many trucks and so many men," and so that a record or report is kept, or but does he just go in and take it by dint of his rank?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In principle, all activities are planned if they can be planned unless they are sudden situations, unexpected situations, contingencies. And in regular procedures, one should act in the way you indicated in your question, that is, you would request an asset from the command that has the decision-making powers. The command approves and orders execution of the task and that is how things are kept under control. However --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: So the command would normally -- normally the command would know. The command of a brigade would know that the Main Staff was requisitioning certain of its assets to perform a task of the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If we're talking about regular operations which had been planned in the system of command. However, on the battlefront, there are situations which are not regular and which cannot be foreseen and sometimes things have to be done ad hoc, without fully respecting the chain of command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: If they have to be done ad hoc in an emergency situation, would the Main Staffers just be able to go and take the order of the people from the brigade to come with them, the equipment, or would they still have to at least file something or communicate with the command of the brigade to let them know they were doing this so that they didn't suddenly find 15 of their trucks weren't there any more or 50 of their men weren't there any more? Would there be any obligation, even in an emergency, to at least inform the regular command that they were requisitioning their material for their own tasks?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In order to use the assets of subordinates in emergency, in emergencies, the authority of the superior is quite sufficient.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Okay, thank you. I've got three or four more questions and I'll be done. You mentioned when we were discussing the evacuation out of Potocari that I think you concluded, and you can correct me if I'm wrong, that this was an evacuation which the civilian representatives themselves wanted. They wanted to get their people out of Potocari and over into the Muslim territory. And I believe at one point you said that the civilian representatives sought the meetings which were held with General Mladic and many other people in the Hotel Fontana on the 10th and 11th. And I'm wondering if you would just very briefly go over your basis for that. My perplexity arises from the fact of the videos that we have seen of the Fontana Hotel meetings would show General Mladic saying "Bring me the representatives of the 28th Division." Twice he said, "I want to have these meetings," to the civilian representatives. "You bring to me these representatives of the 28th Division." And General Krstic himself testified he wondered at the meeting that he was present how those civilians were supposed to be able to bring the representatives of the 28th Division. So the general impression that was left by the videos could well be that these were meetings that were called on the initiative of General Mladic, and that it wasn't something that the civilians were seeking. If you could just briefly give me your reasons for thinking to the contrary.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I base that statement on several facts. The first fact is that the forces of the 28th Division, in defending the enclave, did not show and prove that they wanted to retain control over the enclave by a decisive defence, so that this population had their reservations vis-a-vis the 28th Division. Sometime on the 9th, this was followed up by an initiative of the representative of the civilian population of Srebrenica, the civilian authorities, and sought contacts with the VRS in order to move out the population, evacuate the population. And I did not claim in my statements that the choice to evacuate, that this was not caused by the fear of the consequences of a war. Of course fear played a role there, but on the part of the representatives of the civilian authorities, they did launch the initiative to have the population evacuated, probably for reasons of fear as well. So I don't actually have any illusions that fear did not play a part. Fear did play a part, a significant one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Thank you. I have two more questions and then I'll be done. Now, when a commander, a commander of a corps, or commander of a -- yeah, of a corps, is at a forward command post -- let's say he's in charge of an operation, there's combat operations; he's set up a forward command post. This is the commander of the corps now. Now, even though a combat operation is going on and he's running it, as it were, from the combat -- from the forward command post, are we to expect that he will have established communication facilities sufficient so that he will be able to get reports from all the other parts of his command where he can't be physically present, and even outside information about what's happening to the civilians, what the enemy is saying, all of the kind of information you would think that the commander of a corps would need to know? I mean, can we assume when a commander is at a forward command post, if he is commander of the entire corps, he will be set up to get all of the reports of what's going on in the rest of his area of responsibility? Would that be militarily the objective?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure I understood your question fully, so please excuse me if I am not going to answer what you actually asked me. I'll go back to that. But the forward command posts are established, are formed, for only given assignments to be implemented effectively and efficiently, that means for the operations for which it is indispensable to be able to command from a forward command post. They do not always have to be formed. And in that case, the number of communications are reduced towards that forward command post, that is to say, those which could hamper the effectiveness of the command communications in the operation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Okay. Let me try to rephrase it. Let's assume the commander of the corps -- I don't care whether we assume at the moment it was General Krstic or we assume it was still General Zivanovic. Okay. He's running the Zepa -- he, whichever one is commander, is running the operation from the command post, but he's still the commander of the Drina Corps and all of the area that it entails. My question is simply, would you expect that, even though he was at a forward command post running the particular combat operation, he would have the facilities in place so that he would be getting the regular reports he would need to know what was going on in the rest of the area of his responsibility, as well as any outside information about the activities of civilians or the UN or the outside world that you would expect him to need to know in order to still be the commander of the corps?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, because the possibility of simultaneous communication in the system of command is considered to be an optimum number -- an optimum number of communications is between five and seven. That means that the commander at the same time can have operational contacts and commands with five to seven lines. Over and above that, the system of command does not function properly. It is stifled. And that is why a forward command post is set up to limit the number of information coming in to the forward command post, and all other information which is not relevant, sufficiently relevant for that particular operation that is being undertaken from the forward command post are redirected to the basic command post. And then that is where they are analysed to see whether they are urgent or not. If they are urgent, deemed urgent, they are dispatched to the forward command post; if not, they wait for his return. So they don't go towards the forward command post directly, except the ones directly linked to the operation being undertaken.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: So somebody, somebody at the regular command headquarters, not the forward, makes a decision as to whether or not a communication is important enough to send on to the commander in the forward command post, right? Somebody has to make that decision. If all of the reports are coming in to the regular command post, somebody has to make the decision as to what goes over to the commander at the forward command post, right?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the command post is never without people, left without people who are able to command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Okay, all right, all right. Now my very last question is the following: You have made your case for believing that General Krstic did not become commander until the handover ceremony on August 20th [sic]. I want you for just a moment to assume, assume the opposite just as the predicate for a question. Let's just assume that in fact, as the Prosecution has itself tried to prove, he did become the commander on, let's say, July 13th, I think is the date they used. Would your assessment of his lack of responsibility for anything that happened after that date be changed at all if in fact he had become the commander as of the 13th? Would that change - and if so, how - your assessment of his lack of responsibility for any of the ensuing events after that? In short, would that change your assessment of the total responsibility situation, if he had become commander on the 13th?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not essentially. And this is why: For responsibility, it is essential to know whether he could have known what was happening in the broader area of responsibility. If we bear in mind my answer to your previous question on the reduction of information, then he truly could not have known. But whether he has to know or not, that is up to legal qualifications and not operational qualifications for which I am professionally competent. I am not competent in the legal field. I don't think it would be -- essentially or substantially change my vision of viewing the responsibility of the General Krstic because, at that time, he was at Zepa.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Just to follow that up with one follow-up question. In short, to make sure I understand your answer, if he had been the commander on the 13th and was at Zepa running the -- getting ready for and running the Zepa operation and everything else happened just as it happened down in the rest of the area of responsibility of the Drina Corps, you don't think that, one, he would have been likely to have received information about what was going on in those parts as commander; and, two, that he would not have a greater responsibility to follow up or even make initial inquiries as to what was happening in the rest of the area had he been the commander and not, as you posit, just the operational commander of the Zepa part?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Had he been the corps commander, it could have happened that he could leave his deputy at the forward command post and then go personally to tour the zone of possibility, and then possibly he could have become acquainted with the events in the broader zone. But for as long as he was at the forward command post, information did not reach him except from the units within the composition that was engaged towards Zepa. So in that sense, I consider that it wouldn't -- I wouldn't change my stand -- position with regard to responsibility substantially because, for me, it was important whether he could have known when the actual events took place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Professor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Judge Wald. Judge Fouad Riad, I think you have a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Mr. President, thank you. I would like to dissipate some confusion which your answers -- something said to my colleague Judge Wald. Of course you were speaking as a Professor and she called you a Professor. I want you to speak to me as a General in a specific army. Now, you said in order to use -- I'm quoting you: "In order to use in emergencies, the order of the superior is quite sufficient." Now, applying this to our situation, it means that the Main Staff could help himself, could help himself and grab anything from the Drina Corps when they wanted it, being superior? Just in a few words, is it possible to happen without even coordination or information?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They have that right, but it is assumed that they would have informed somebody. It is the right of the commander to utilise resources, assets.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Either the Drina Corps or the other corps would have been having other plans and then they come and just grab their transport or -- their transportations or anything. Wouldn't that cause a real - What can I say? - disturbance even in the execution plan of the corps? Is it within the military discipline?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Superior Command coordinates the work of subordinates and it has the right to set the priorities. So it can, according to its right of command to utilise any resource, but it is implied that this goes through the commander, through the system of command, except in emergencies when the whole chain of command is not functioning properly and there are certain deviations. And as we saw in this operation, these were frequent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Another thing you said was that the subordinate must not execute the order which violates the law and that he can, if need be, surpass his command and report to the higher -- to the highest or to the higher authorities. Now, practically speaking, if he knows -- the subordinate knows that it is a policy that is being executed, what could be his reaction and what would be the risks he takes? Practically speaking, not as a Professor.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Practically speaking, one can ask for an explanation that he be told why this is being done. He can caution of the consequences. He can write a document to the superior, requesting that he be relieved of the execution of the order and he can resign, simply give up his position if he does not wish to have a part in it. And the worst consequence is to lose his life, and it's better to sacrifice one's life than one's honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me for interrupting, but there's a problem with the transcript for some time now. What's happening?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Registrar, tell us what's happening, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I spoke with the technical booth and they said they're working on it right now and it will take a couple of minutes to fix.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You suggested a break. That is when I said it could be sabotage. How much time do we need? I think it's working now. Good.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Your answer, General, is extremely enlightening, but without asking somebody to be a hero and sacrifice his life, as you said, in a regular army, in particular this regular army, was there any danger of sacrificing one's life if you resigned or if you bring up the violation? Was there a real risk?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm really not able to answer that question whether there was such a risk or not. I really don't know. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Judge Fouad Riad.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: [Intepretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, Krivaja 95, we already know that its objective was to essentially separate the two enclaves of Zepa and Srebrenica and reduce them in size. So to attack Srebrenica was not part of the plan. If I tell you that such an operation would have required preparations lasting 20 to 30 days, what would be your reaction?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would say that it wouldn't need 20 to 30 days. It would need less time, but certainly more time than was used.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I tell you that the person who made this statement was precisely the person who planned Krivaja 95, that is, General Krstic, would you revise your response or would you abide by it?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't because I know how operations are planned, just like General Krstic, because this was command staff who were directly in the area of responsibility. There are no great marches that require a long time for the movement. They were units that were in contact. They were units from the area. They were people who were mostly familiar with the area. And except for the materiel side, replenishment of fuel, supplies, armaments, logistical development, in that sense more time would be needed if such a radical operation was involved. But I think a month is too long. For the actual preparation of the preparation for bringing in the forces and deploying them wouldn't need so much time, but General Krstic probably bore in mind the condition in which the corps was, their equipment, their materiel, their ammunitions. So he felt that, for the reinforcement and replenishment, he would need more time, but not in terms of the staff actually.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Another question, General. You have told us there wasn't a town or village, a Serb town or village in Podrinje. What period are you referring to when you say that?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm referring to the 7th of January, 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So on that date there wasn't a town or village occupied by the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On that day, the last Serb village in Central Podrinje was captured.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. But how do you combine the defensive nature of the VRS, how do you reconcile it with the attack on Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is nothing unusual there or strange.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry for interrupting you, but you did say that the objective of the VRS was not to conquer territory which was not Serb territory.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I said that the army of Republika Srpska or, rather, its political strategy had in mind their own ethnic territory, a vision of their own territory. It is questionable whether they were right, but when they reached those borders with their army, the borders of the territory which they laid claim on without entering into whether they were right or not, then they switched to a strategic defensive. They captured defensive positions, which meant holding on to defensive lines. But Republika Srpska had a very small population. It still has a small population. So after that, they never carried out a single offensive operation which would mean capturing additional territory beyond those borders which they had taken possession of. Within that territory where the VRS has a strategy of defence, so it no longer has any further ambitions, nor does it believe it should conquer fresh territory, there were certain areas that were still under the control of the Muslim army, such as the enclaves. Within the territory that they considered their ethnic territory, they did engage in military actions which were tactically of an offensive nature. One such action is Krivaja 95.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, General. We have discussed at length the number of soldiers of the 28th Division, as you will remember probably. You said that you took Muslim documents because they were more reliable, and you added they had no reason lie to their commanders. Do you remember saying that?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was referring to the Muslim commanders, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Take the example of the intercepts. When the soldiers or the technicians were intercepting radio communications in order to inform their superiors, their commanders, do you think they -- that they had a reason to lie to their commanders?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You have asked me a question which it is difficult for me to answer logically without making an error. Theoretically speaking, they need not have, but they could have lied. They could have presented the situation as being more dramatic than it was, that they were more exposed, that they were holding on better than they were. This is possible, but it need not be so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But do you think that these persons who are doing this work, were they or not fully aware of the importance of their information for the decisions to be taken by the commanders; so if they lied to their commanders, they are exposing themselves to danger? What do you think about that?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, I said that the Muslim leaders and commanders from Srebrenica more correctly reported about their own effectives than did the soldiers of the VRS in their estimates based on intelligence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not talking about that information. I'm talking about intercepts, intercepted communications that you have read. You said that you have read all of them, and in detail. But theoretically, those people who were doing that job, do you believe that it was in their interests to tell the truth to their commanders, or do you think that they may have deliberately lied to their commanders? It is this type of information that I am referring to.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I personally think that it would be more realistic to expect them not to lie than to lie.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have another question. Did the VRS intercept radio communications of the enemy army, if I may call it that?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All armies do that, so I assume that they did, too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. How did they use those intercepts?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They are used in intelligence work, but they are never used with a high level of reliability. They always have to be verified.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I have some shorter questions now. Do you know what was the time required for the handing over of duty between corps commanders and his deputy?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If we're talking about people belonging to the same command, if it is the same command, then it doesn't take long. It can be done in an hour, in a day. But the normal procedure would be for the old and the new commander to tour the units on the occasion of the handing over the duty, when that is possible. When it is not possible, it's not done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, another question. Is it possible to make a distinction between a de jure position and a de facto position? For example, General Krstic could have been the corps commander and have the official ceremony subsequently to confirm that position; or, in other words, is it possible for the Supreme Commander of the army to give a verbal order, "I designate you the corps commander," to issue a decree later, and still later to have the ceremony? Is that possible in theory, according to the rules?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, that is not possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Imagine that the commander falls ill and he's unable to exercise his duties. What happens from the standpoint of his replacement?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Automatically his duties are taken over by the Chief of Staff, that is, his deputy. So that excludes the possibility of having hasty decisions because this system has already been built into the system, that is, of the Chief of Staff being the deputy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So is it possible for General Krstic de facto to be the acting corps commander because somebody has said to Zivanovic, You cannot -- "You go, and the commander will replace you"; having verified this, the decree is published, and after that, the official ceremony is held? Would that be possible from the legal standpoint?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Legally, no. It is only possible if you wish to violate the law.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Why not? If the Deputy Commander automatically replaces him, why not legally?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is automatic when the commander is unable for personal or other reasons to execute his task.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that is my hypothesis. He is prevented by somebody telling him, "You go." General Mladic could have said that, President Karadzic could have said that, or not?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is no need to do that when a decree on appointment can be issued quickly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, General, I have another question. Why was General Zivanovic replaced in the middle of the war? Why should a corps commander be replaced; can you imagine a reason?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know of any reason.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but on the basis of your military expertise, doesn't it seem to you to be strange to replace a corps commander, and then also to discuss which is the most convenient date for the ceremony? Because, after all, the war is continuing. Why? When General Zivanovic is not urgently needed for another position, why? Don't you find that strange?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Personnel changes are made in wartime, Your Honour. There are appointments, changes on the personnel -- in the personnel structure. This is also normal in wartime. There is a personnel service in wartime. The Main Staff of the VRS had assistant corps commanders for personnel matters, and lists are made, forecasts of personnel development, and the best combinations are made in terms of personnel. In the process of these personnel changes, it was decided that General Krstic should become corps commander. There is nothing strange in that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, that is your opinion and your position. As a military man, as an expert, a military expert, how do you view General Krstic's career? Did he -- was he promoted quickly or slowly?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Neither quickly nor slowly. I was a younger general than he was. Even though it was peacetime, I became a general at a younger age than he did. It was not an extremely successful career nor an unsuccessful career.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But in any event, can it be said that the promotion to the position of corps commander was, in a sense - I don't know how to put it - a way of remunerating or recognising his good work in the previous period? Could we reason it that way?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unsuccessful people are certainly not appointed to be commanders, that's the first principle. People who are successful in their positions are appointed to such positions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Are there any other conditions to be promoted? Are there any other conditions to be promoted, for instance, those linked to the Security Service, anything to do with the Security Service?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The principle in the army I served in, and a very similar doctrine was adopted by the VRS, that the Chief of Staff, the outgoing Chief of Staff should be appointed to the commander, precisely in order to more easily adjust to his new position. So one of the conditions is success, ability, and the previous position that he held which qualifies him for that duty, which means being Chief of Staff. Also, he needs to have a certain education and training behind him for that position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but we heard people here in the courtroom who told us that the opinion of the Security Service was required. If someone was successful and the Security Service was against it, he couldn't be promoted. Are you aware of that? Is that true or not?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Security Service does not verify expertise. It does not have the ability to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But what does it verify? I understand not the professional qualities of the person, but tell me what the Security Service does verify as a precondition for a senior officer to be promoted.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In armies in democratic societies, the Security Service does not have that role, but in ideologized and politicised systems the Security Service does screen people which in normal armies should not be done. Unfortunately, this also applied to the army I served in and also in the VRS. This was verified.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So it means that the Security Service did check whether General Krstic met all the requirements for promotion. Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this particular case, I don't know. I cannot tell you. But let me say that the assistant for security of the Superior Command which initiates proposals for personnel is a member of the personnel council of the Main Staff. So he's consulted, as are the other assistant commanders. Secondly, that service, by nature of things, as in a certain sense a Secret Service, can act outside the institutional structure to speed up somebody's promotion or to slow down somebody's promotion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you, General. I would also like to have a final question for you. I don't know -- I don't want to know whether you answered my learned friend Madam Wald as a professor, but Judge Riad asked you to answer in your capacity as general, which means you have both qualifications. You are a professor and you are also a general. At the end of your expert testimony, do you feel that you referred more to your qualities as a professor or to your qualities as a general? Which did you rely on most in your testimony?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You really put me in a dilemma, but I shall take the liberty to give you an answer. My career as a professor and my studies and the references I required in that area of my life made it possible for me to address this problem better as a general. So it helped me. Therefore, in this Court, in this honourable Tribunal, I testified in the first place as a general, but being a professor, I did my best to make recourse to all my knowledge and all the means available to me through that career to address this predominantly military problem as best I could. To what extent I was successful it is up to you to judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I see that Judge Riad has another question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Actually, it's a question that follows on a reply that you gave to the President. In any event, I have to comment on what you said. You're a general but you have all the art of a professor. I was a professor all my life and I can see you are a true professor. In the reply that you gave to the President, and I'm almost quoting what you said, you said the rules do not allow a commander to assume powers de facto prior to his official appointment and that is normal when you were speaking as a professor and talking about regular conditions. But now, in a practical situation, if - it is a hypothesis - if a commander is not well seen, is more or less a persona non grata by the authorities, and he's going to be replaced, doesn't that successor de facto play an important role? Of course, if it is according to the rules, then it is de jure, but I'm talking a de facto situation when the commander is suspect and not in people's good books. What would be your comment, as a hypothesis?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You want me to speak as a general or as a professor?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You are both at the same time, because after all, the professor does not live in an ivory tower. He has to have his feet on the ground.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I would act as a general and I would replace the commander who I consider not to be appropriate for the position he holds. Therefore, I would not be guided by my personal feelings but by his abilities. If a corps commander is not suited to that position, I would replace him immediately, and I would inform my personnel officials to draw up a decree, to make that decree public immediately that a commander is being replaced and a new one appointed, this on condition that that is my position. If that is not my position, if I consider that someone else would be a better solution than the person in office, then I would wait for more favourable conditions and do it through the regular procedure without provoking any kind of a personnel incident. There cannot be any discontinuity in command because there are deputies who can take over the duties normally. So the legislator has made sure that the system functions automatically, regardless of whether the person who nominally has a position is present or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: One more question, but I relieve you of the obligation to answer if you don't want to. The appointment of General Krstic as a commander, according to your research, and you were there, was there any opposition between the leaders over that appointment, that is, between Karadzic and Mladic, in your opinion? And this could have slowed down the official nomination.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think there was no disagreement whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: It provoked one last question, Professor/General. If you were, in fact, the appointing authority and you had the authority to appoint the commander of the corps and you really -- hypothetical -- you really thought the present commander was inadequate and you wanted to get a new one on the spot as fast as you could and you were ready to take the full responsibility, would you be able to put out a decree which said, "I am appointing `X' to be the commander effective immediately and I don't want the hand-over period to go into operation, I want this first man out and the second man in immediately," and you had the -- you were the appointing authority, you could do that? Could you dispense with the holdover period and put your new man on the spot effective immediately with the time of the decree if you thought that was the right thing to do for your command?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Supreme Commander has that right too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So, General, it is 3.30. We promised to finish at 3.30. I see that we can't do that. I see that Mr. Visnjic has something to say. The documents that you wish to tender, can we do that tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. I was just -- I just wished to notify you that the witness service has informed us that the General will be staying here tomorrow as well, so we can take advantage of the first ten minutes tomorrow to tender the documents in his presence, if that is required by the Rules of Procedure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think it is not necessary. Mr. Cayley?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, as far as the Defence documents are concerned, I have no objections to any of their documents. I don't know if they have any objection to mine. If there are no objections, then I don't think the General needs to be here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Do you have any objection to the Prosecution documents?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, no, no. We have no objections at all. And we have a list of documents ready, so we can exchange it with the registrar. The lists have already been provided to the registrar, and I can simply ask for the record that the documents on the list be tendered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What I wish to do, Mr. Visnjic, is to adjourn at 3.30 and also to release the witness. Because our aim is not to prolong but rather to release the witness because we were told that he had to leave. So, so long as there are no objections, we can address the matter tomorrow. We do have another witness for tomorrow. Otherwise, I did say that we would be working an extra half hour; otherwise, we can go on for a whole hour. So we can do that tomorrow. So please be seated for us to say good-bye to the witness. I don't know how to call you now, "General" or "Professor" or both. I have taken note of the fact that you had a dilemma here. I think you had a trilemma because, in addition to your qualifications as a professor and a general, you have a certain problem with your voice. But I think you have contributed to eliminate this stigma that you spoke of, the stigma that all the Serbs have as a result of these events. I think you have the words and the throat to contribute to the process of peace, as you have done here, and I thank you very much, General and Professor, for having come and for having clarified many questions and many matters on which we have to decide. So I wish you a happy journey back to your country, and much success in your work on peace, pacification, and reconstruction. Thank you, General, and thank you, Professor. Thank you.
